title: 'Like gods reigning over humans': Many defectors see daughter of North Korea's Kim as heir apparent

sections.title: Conversation 1
sections.scene: A university student and her professor discuss a research paper on hereditary succession in authoritarian states.

script.en: Professor, I've been reading about how some authoritarian regimes manage power transitions, and I'm struck by how often family succession appears. Is that really a common pattern?

It is more common than many people assume, though it takes different forms. In some cases, a ruling family prepares a child for leadership from an early age, introducing them at military events and state ceremonies. The idea is to signal continuity to elites and the public.
But doesn't that create resentment? I'd imagine ordinary citizens might question why one family should hold power indefinitely.

Resentment certainly exists, but it is rarely expressed openly. In highly controlled societies, public dissent is severely punished, so people often keep their views private. What we see instead is quiet adaptation—people finding ways to survive within the system.
So how do researchers study public opinion in such closed countries? Surveys would be unreliable, wouldn't they?

Exactly. That's why some scholars rely on interviews with defectors who still have contacts inside the country. It's not a perfect method—the sample is small and potentially biased—but it offers rare insight into private attitudes.
I see. And what about the role of gender? I noticed that in some cases a female heir is treated with skepticism.

That's an important point. Deeply patriarchal traditions can make a female successor appear less legitimate to some observers, even when official propaganda promotes her. But we should be careful not to assume that such attitudes are universal.
So for my paper, I should focus on how succession is signaled publicly rather than trying to measure private opinion directly?

That would be a sensible approach. Analyze the ceremonies, the media language, and the protocols. Those observable signals can tell you a great deal about a regime's intentions, even if the public's true feelings remain hidden.

script.en: For decades, scholars of authoritarian politics have debated how dictatorships manage the transfer of power, a question that remains central to understanding the durability of nondemocratic rule. Unlike democracies, where leadership changes are regulated by elections and constitutional rules, personalist regimes often lack clear procedures for deciding who will rule next. This uncertainty can make succession a moment of considerable risk, both for the ruling elite and for ordinary citizens, because any miscalculation may trigger instability or even violence. One strategy that some regimes adopt is to groom a family member as the designated heir, thereby keeping power within a trusted circle. By introducing the chosen successor at military parades, weapons tests, and national ceremonies, the leadership sends a visible message that the existing order will continue. Such appearances are carefully staged: the heir is placed beside the leader, greeted with exaggerated deference by senior officials, and described in state media with language normally reserved for the country's highest authority. Yet public displays of favor do not guarantee a smooth transition, since they may intensify rather than resolve underlying tensions. Analysts note that succession can provoke factional rivalry, particularly when the heir is young or inexperienced and therefore lacks an independent power base. also, in societies with strong patriarchal traditions, a female successor may face doubts about her legitimacy, even if official propaganda promotes her prominently. These doubts are rarely voiced openly, but they can influence how elites calculate their interests. Because such regimes restrict independent polling and punish dissent, researchers face serious obstacles in gauging popular sentiment. Some rely on interviews with defectors who maintain contacts inside the country, while others analyze observable signals such as media coverage and ceremonial protocol. Neither approach is flawless, but together they offer a partial window into a largely opaque political world. What emerges is a picture of succession as a process that is carefully managed in public yet deeply uncertain beneath the surface.

sections.title: The Politics of Succession in a Closed Regime
sections.passage:
North Korea allows no dissent and harshly punishes attempts to flee the country. Established in 1948, the nation is nominally a socialist republic, but in reality it is an authoritarian dynasty, with three generations of the Kim family ruling in succession. There was no known public resistance during its previous two successions—from state founder Kim Il Sung to his son Kim Jong Il in 1994 and then from Kim Jong Il to his son Kim Jong Un in 2011. The question of who will become the next leader is crucial because that person will face a huge challenge: governing an impoverished, nuclear-armed nation whose 26 million people have little political freedom and live under strict state surveillance while being cut off from much of the outside world.

Since late 2022, Kim Jong Un's daughter has made dozens of public appearances, all of them with her father at big events like weapons tests and military parades. State media has called her Kim's "most beloved" and "respected" child. Her status has been emphasized by images showing an elderly general kneeling before her and her standing in front of her father. South Korea's spy agency says she is Kim's likely heir. Eight of the 11 defectors interviewed by the Associated Press shared that view; the others disagreed, citing the North's deeply patriarchal culture.

"During her visits to missile launch sites and factories, the way senior North Korean officials treat Kim Ju Ae involves protocols reserved for a successor, not the ones simply for a daughter of Kim Jong Un," said Tae Yongho, a former minister at North Korea's Embassy in London who defected to South Korea in 2016. "They are repeating the same protocol and treatment they provided for Kim Jong Un" when he accompanied his father as his heir.

Much of the skepticism about Kim Ju Ae as a potential leader stems from her being female. South Korean officials believe she has a younger sibling whose gender hasn't been confirmed. Women in North Korea remain deeply underrepresented in senior posts. Only one of 17 department directors for the ruling Workers' Party is a woman. That woman is Kim Jong Un's influential younger sister, Kim Yo Jong, according to South Korea's Unification Ministry.

"My contacts in North Korea say it would be nonsensical to revere that little girl as their supreme leader," said Kim Jeong-Ah, a former North Korean army officer who resettled in South Korea in 2009. Such remarks illustrate how hereditary succession remains a subject of quiet contention, even as the regime stages elaborate ceremonies to signal continuity. The public choreography of power may suggest certainty, but beneath the surface, the question of who will rule next remains unsettled.
